title: The routes around competition, and how much went down each
question: Which rules let a department skip competitive bidding, and how much has been paid under each since fiscal 2019?
finding: From fiscal 2019 to fiscal 2026 the City paid $4.08 billion under rules that set competition aside: $1.49 billion under emergency powers, $1.52 billion as sole source, $761.8 million where an ordinance waives bidding and $303.0 million under other "not bid" rules. That is 7.5% of the $54.52 billion of payments that record any rule; 51% of all payment dollars record none. The total peaked at $703.4 million in fiscal 2021 and was $695.4 million in fiscal 2026, when payments under ordinance waivers ($394.5 million) had replaced most of the emergency spending.
how: Every line of the Controller’s vendor-payment file carries the purchasing rule staff keyed for it. Each distinct wording was sorted into a route: emergency; sole source; the Health Department’s sole-source list; bidding waived by ordinance; other wordings that say "not bid" or "no bid"; and small purchases departments may make themselves. Agreements with other public bodies and purchases through a hospital buying consortium are left out. Payments are added up by the fiscal year (July to June) in which each was issued, which is read from its voucher number and not from the year the file lists it under; contracts are those in the Supplier Contracts table that started on or after 1 July 2018. Shares are of payments that record a rule.
limits: Each of these routes is written into the Administrative Code with a stated condition: a real emergency, a real single source, a class of work the Board has excused from bidding. The rule is whatever staff keyed and about half of payment dollars carry none, so these are floors. A "not bid" wording can cover work chosen from a pre-qualified pool. Emergency spending in fiscal 2020 to 2022 is mostly the pandemic response. The payment file labels each line with a fiscal year that is not always the year the payment was issued: some earlier payments, mostly on purchase orders in multi-year capital funds, are filed under a later year, and the Controller's own published figures follow that label. Payments are dated here by voucher number, a single running sequence, which moves $5.52 billion of $119.3 billion (4.6%) to an earlier year than its label; $1.08 billion of that belongs to fiscal 2018 or earlier, before the file starts. Near the turn of a year the number dates a payment to within a few days. Payments that belong to fiscal 2018 or earlier are in none of the figures here. Under the rules shown here that comes to $51.5 million.
